headings: Professor Josep Torrellas Thomas M. Siebel Chair in Computer Science, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign Director, SRC/DARPA JUMP 2.0 ACE Center for Evolvable Computing (torrella@illinois.edu) Google Scholar, CV May 2026

Looking for Graduate Students: If interested, please send an email with your CV to torrella@illinois.edu. JOSEP TORRELLAS BIO: Professor Josep Torrellas is the Thomas M. Siebel Chair in Computer Science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). He is the Director of the SRC/DARPA JUMP 2.0 ACE Center for Evolvable Computing . He has made contributions to computer architectures for shared-memory multiprocessor memory systems and thread-level speculation (TLS). Torrellas' early work on false sharing helped understand shared-data behavior in multiprocessor caches. Researchers and practitioners in architecture and compilers built on its insights. Further, his analyses of how operating systems and commercial workloads exercise multiprocessor caches grounded the work of subsequent researchers. Torrellas has made contributions to memory systems of multiprocessor architectures, including NUMA organizations, coherence protocols, and prefetching schemes. In recognition, the government made his I-ACOMA multiprocessor one of the Ten Design-Point Studies funded nationwide to attain Petascale-level machines. Torrellas' work on TLS, spanning two decades, provided substantial breadth and depth on the topic. He developed new parallel architectures and schemes for thread commit, out-of-order thread spawning, and dependence-violation elimination. He built a TLS compiler and introduced a taxonomy of eager and lazy buffering of speculative state. Torrellas expanded the application of TLS to parallel codes. He used them to avoid synchronization stalls (Speculative Synchronization), provide fault-tolerance (ReVive), debug data races (ReEnact), monitor memory (I-Watcher), and enforce sequential consistency cheaply (BulkSC). Some of his TLS ideas were adopted in IBM's Blue Gene supercomputer and other industrial designs, and influenced work on transactional memory. TLS concepts were central to his Bulk Multiprocessor architecture. A BulkCompiler transformed code into speculative atomic blocks called Chunks. Then, cores continuously executed Chunks while enforcing cache coherence using bulk operations on address sets encoded with Bloom filters. The Bulk architecture constituted a novel execution model. TLS principles inspired his work on Record and deterministic Replay (RnR). Torrellas contributed with designs for performance, software debugging, and security. Together with Intel, he built the first RnR hardware prototype (QuickRec) . Torrellas worked on multiple industrial prototypes. He was in the design team of IBM's PERCS Multiprocessor , which considered some of his TLS mechanisms and processing-in-memory features inspired by his FlexRAM Intelligent Memory project. Later, Torrellas also worked in Intel's Runnemede Extreme-Scale Multiprocessor . The project built on his contributions in energy-efficient architectures. They include the VARIUS model of process variation, and techniques to minimize and tolerate process variation. Torrellas was also involved in the Stanford DASH and Illinois Cedar experimental multiprocessors Torrellas has received the IEEE CS Harry H. Goode Memorial Award , the UIUC College of Engineering Daniel C. Drucker Eminent Faculty Award, the IEEE CS Technical Achievement Award , the UIUC Campus Award for Excellence in Graduate Student Mentoring, a Willett Faculty Fellowship at UIUC, and many Best Paper and High-Impact Paper awards. He is a Fellow of IEEE, ACM, and AAAS. Torrellas has led multiple large research efforts with industry. Since 2023, he has been the Director of the SRC/DARPA JUMP 2.0 ACE Center for Evolvable Computing . He leads 21 faculty from 13 US universities in their collaboration with 15 SRC companies. He has contributed with new energy-efficient multiprocessor computer architectures. In 2018-2021, he was a co-Leader of a 5-PI Intel Strategic Research Alliance (ISRA) Center on Computer Security . He developed pipeline and cache microarchitectures to thwart speculative-execution attacks. In 2011-2013, he was the Director of the Illinois-Intel Parallelism Center (I2PC) , a center with 17 faculty PIs, focused on designing computer architectures and software for parallelism. Torrellas has had two stints as Chair of the IEEE Technical Community on Computer Architecture (TCCA) , in 2005-2010 and 2018-2022. He has served as a Member of the Board of Directors of the Computing Research Association (CRA) , and as a Council Member of the Computing Community Consortium (CCC) from CRA. In 2018-2023, he served as a Member of the U.S. National Academies Board on Army Research and Development (BOARD) , and since 2016, as Member of the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS) . In 2010, he co-organized two workshops on Revitalizing Computer Architecture that impacted the creation of the NSF's Scalable Parallelism in the Extreme (SPX) Program. What Torrellas enjoys the most is working with his graduate students.
He has graduated 53 PhDs, of which 23 are currently in academia. Fifteen of them are professors at US research universities: Martinez (Cornell), Solihin (UCF), Huang (Rochester), Prvulovic (Gatech), Renau (UCSC), Tuck (NCSU), Ceze (Washington), Teodorescu (OSU), Muzahid (Texas A&M), Karpuzcu (Minnesota), Yan (MIT), Pothukuchi (UNC-Chapel Hill), Skarlatos (CMU), Zhao (UT-Austin), and Stojkovic (UT-Austin). Torrellas received a PhD from Stanford University. « Publications » « Curr. Vitae » « Students Graduated »

Torrellas leads The i-acoma Architecture Group , which focuses on new processor, 
          memory, and system technologies and organizations to build novel multiprocessor 
          computer architectures. Two examples of projects we have done in the past: A novel multicore architecture for programmability: The Bulk Multicore Architecture (Communications of the ACM,
                 December 2009). [Presentation slides]. EE Times article that discusses the Bulk Multicore. Dr. Dobb's Journal discussion of the Bulk Multicore. Making Parallel Programming Easy: Research Contributions from Illinois, a book

                 ground up for energy and power efficiency: Thrifty: An Extreme-Scale Multiprocessor Architecture (IEEE Computer, November 2009). [Presentation slides].
